Apple's market share reached 22 per cent, crossing 20 per cent for the first time in a third quarter, despite a year-on-year decline in shipments. The absence of a base iPhone 18 model resulted in a smaller launch-month channel fill than the full iPhone 17 lineup a year earlier, Counterpoint said. OPPO and vivo recorded shipment declines of more than 20 per cent. Xiaomi saw a more than 30 per cent fall, reducing its market share to 10 per cent as the company cut exposure to lower-priced devices and some overseas markets to protect margins. "The outlook for the remainder of 2026 remains challenging," Counterpoint said. "Production cuts, tighter portfolios, and greater focus on premium devices are likely to continue, while price-sensitive segments face further pressure from higher device prices and limited availability of components."

Source: Reuters

item.title: サウジ首都の空港が閉鎖延長、フーシ派攻撃で被害 経済への影響懸念
item.description:
Gianluca Lo Nostro Menna AlaaElDin
［１２日 ロイター］ -
item.dc:creator: ロイター
item.content:encoded:
Gianluca Lo Nostro　Menna AlaaElDin

［１２日　ロイター］ - サウジアラビア当局は１２日、週末にイエメンの親イラン武装組織フーシ派の攻撃を受けた首都リヤドのキング・ハリド国際空港の運用停止措置を１７日まで延長した。

サウジ民間航空当局は、空港閉鎖について、「空港施設の安全と運用準備態勢を確保するための手続きを完了させる」ためだと説明した。同空港の利用者数は、ジッダに次いで国内２番目に多い。

フーシ派は１２日夜、弾道ミサイルで同空港を攻撃したと発表した。これに先立ち、サウジ側は、フーシ派がリヤドに向けて発射した弾道ミサイルを迎撃・破壊したと発表していた。

フーシ派は声明で、サウジ南西部ハミスムシャイトの空軍基地もドローン（無人機）で攻撃したと表明した。これについてサウジ側は現時点で確認していない。

１２日に発出された航空情報（ＮＯＴＡＭ）によると、キング・ハリド国際空港は１０月１７日２１００ＧＭＴ（日本時間１８日午前６時）まで閉鎖される。

同空港は１０日の攻撃以降、閉鎖されている。この攻撃では１３人が死亡、３００人超が負傷し、サウジ国内では過去１０年以上で最も多くの死者を出した。１１日の別の攻撃では１人が死亡し、十数人が負傷した。

一連の攻撃は、サウジ航空業界に混乱をもたらすとともに、航空燃料の高騰に直面している航空会社にさらなる打撃となっている。

航空機追跡サイト「フライトレーダー２４」のデータによると、航空機は１２日、リヤドを避けて飛行している。ただ、サウジ領空を通過し、西海岸の主要拠点であるジッダに着陸する便は見られた。

航空データ分析会社シリウムによると、サウジ国内の全空港での欠航率は４６．４％に達した。

混乱を受けて欧州やアジアの航空各社は運航停止を余儀なくされている。欧州航空安全庁（ＥＡＳＡ）は９日、ミサイルやドローンによる攻撃を理由に、サウジ領空に関する警告の対象範囲を拡大した。米連邦航空局（ＦＡＡ）は１１日、米国の航空会社に対し、サウジへの飛行や領空通過の際に警戒するよう勧告した。

ルフトハンザ・グループはリヤド便を１０月１６日まで全便欠航とし、エールフランスＫＬＭはリヤド発着便の運航停止措置を今月末まで延長した。

アブダビのエティハド航空もサウジ便の欠航延長を決めた。

デルタ航空は、当初１０月２３日に予定していたアトランタ─リヤド線の就航を２０２７年３月まで延期すると発表した。

今回の攻撃は、今月リヤドで開催予定の大規模会合にも影を落とす。世界石油会議（ＷＰＣ）の会合は、複数の石油大手トップが参加を取りやめた。

フーシ派との衝突激化により、より広範な経済的影響への懸念が強まっている。サウジの実質国内総生産（ＧＤＰ）は、石油活動の低迷など複数の要因を反映し、２０２６年に３．６％縮小すると予測されている。

item.title: Saudi Arabia faces new missile and drone fire after major attacks on airports
item.description: Saudi Arabia said it was facing a new barrage of incoming fire on Monday and that Riyadh airport would remain shut for now, days after Saturday's deadly missile strike on a departure terminal that was claimed by Yemen's Iran-allied Houthis.
item.dc:creator: Timour Azhari
item.content:encoded: Saudi Arabia said it was facing a new barrage of incoming fire on Monday and that Riyadh airport would remain shut for now, days after Saturday's deadly [USN:L1N45W03M TEXT:"missile strike"] on a departure terminal that was claimed by Yemen's Iran-allied Houthis. Incoming drones and missiles were reported by the Saudi-led coalition backing government forces in Yemen, though there was no immediate news of whether they were intercepted. The [USN:L1N45Q02Z TEXT:"Houthis"] have been attacking Saudi airports and oil facilities since last week as part of a rapidly escalating conflict that has spilled over from the wider regional conflagration between the United States and Iran . Those attacks have shut down parts of Saudi airspace, [USN:L6N45Y0C1 TEXT:"suspending operations"] at Riyadh airport, and largely emptying the skies over the capital even as the city hosts a major [USN:L6N45Y0GT TEXT:"energy conference"]. Saudi Arabia now faces a nightmare predicament, having [USN:L1N45Q02D TEXT:"re-entered Yemen's civil war"] to push the Houthis from the vital Bab el-Mandeb Strait oil route and stop the group making further gains after its sudden advances in September. With the Yemeni forces Riyadh supports having made some gains against the Houthis around Bab el-Mandeb but still on the back foot on other fronts, Yemeni military sources said, any pressure on the Houthis could take time to pay off. Saudi Arabia's long-time regional rival Iran offered to mediate between its Houthi allies and the kingdom. "We have repeatedly expressed our readiness to help facilitate dialogue between the parties," foreign ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei said on Monday. Meanwhile, despite intensified Saudi airstrikes against the group, including what Yemeni television said were hits on al-Jawf province on Monday, the Houthis show no sign of letting up their own barrage of attacks on Saudi infrastructure. The group has repeatedly threatened to target airports and airspace, as well as Saudi oil installations that provide the engine for the kingdom's economy and its ambitious development plans. UAE CALLS FOR JOINT GULF ACTION Saudi Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman said at Monday's conference that the kingdom would stay focused on bringing in investment as part of its wider economic development goals. "The development of our energy system and industrial capability continues," he said. Saudi Arabia's neighbour the United Arab Emirates on Monday called for a revival of joint Gulf action on security and defence in response to the attacks. UAE presidential adviser Anwar Gargash said the targeting of Saudi Arabia undermined the security of all Gulf states and added that the neglect of collective Gulf security had "emboldened others" to overreach against regional states. Saudi Arabia and the UAE had been partners in the Yemen conflict for years, but they backed different forces within the Yemeni military coalition supporting the government and fell out last winter. US President Donald Trump said on Saturday that Washington was considering joining Saudi Arabia in strikes on the Houthis, but there has been no sign yet of any US action.

item.title: Microsoft plans huge deployment of its own AI chips, with an eye on saving costs
item.description: Microsoft announced the next generation of its custom AI chip on Monday and said it plans to deploy potentially more than a million of them next year to back its internal AI services.
item.dc:creator: Stephen Nellis, Max Cherney
item.content:encoded: Microsoft (MSFT.O) announced the next generation of its custom AI chip on Monday and said it plans to deploy potentially more than a million of them next year to back its internal AI services. The Maia 300, as the chip is called, is the third generation of the company's custom chips designed to handle AI data crunching such as coding and carrying out complex business tasks on a user's behalf. Its predecessor is already running Microsoft's in-house AI models, as well as models from OpenAI delivered on Microsoft's Azure cloud computing service. The new version comes amid a flurry of custom chips from both [USN:L6N45G0UZ TEXT:"cloud computing rivals"] and [USN:L6N42V15J TEXT:"AI firms such as OpenAI"] aimed at loosening the hold of Nvidia (NVDA.O) on the AI computing market. To construct the chip, Microsoft took a different technical path from Nvidia whose AI accelerators use one massive computing chip surrounded by high-bandwidth memory chips. The central computing processor in Microsoft's Maia 300 silicon is composed of "chiplets" — typically specialized chips bonded together — that use 2-nanometer technology from Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co (2330.TW) for key computing functions. Other chiplets included in the design use cheaper 3-nanometer tech for functions such as moving data off the processor and elsewhere inside the system. The Maia 300 processors will go into racks that contain 96 chips and use about 167 kilowatts of power, compared with the 142 kilowatts used by Nvidia's most recent GB300 AI server racks with 72 of its graphics processing units (GPUs). Microsoft said the Maia 300 chips will get about 40% more useful computing done per megawatt than "leading GPU-based systems," though it did not name the systems it used for a comparison. "It's basically delivering more intelligence for every watt, every dollar, and every byte of memory by optimizing across the entire system," Rani Borkar, president of Azure hardware systems and infrastructure at Microsoft, told Reuters in an interview. Microsoft said it plans to roll out "multi-gigawatt deployments" of the Maia 300 chip starting next year. Microsoft has said it [USN:L4N43V23K TEXT:"expects to spend"] more than $175 billion in capital expenditures this calendar year.

item.title: Wall Street’s AI bet is now too big to hit
item.description: The hurdle for continued AI-driven equity gains is strikingly high. And with cracks starting to appear in the seemingly impenetrable tech edifice, there are mounting signs AI risk is now far more than just a case of "bad vibes."
item.dc:creator: Jamie McGeever
item.content:encoded: The hurdle for continued AI-driven equity gains is strikingly high. And with cracks starting to appear in the seemingly impenetrable tech edifice, there are mounting signs AI risk is now far more than just a case of "bad vibes." While the S&P 500 (.SPX) and Nasdaq (.IXIC) climbed to fresh highs last week, a string of negative headlines related to AI – from a shelved initial public offering (IPO) in Australia to reports that ChatGPT maker OpenAI's revenue is [USN:L4N45U1QQ TEXT:"falling short"] of earlier estimates – suggests markets could soon run into some serious obstacles. Earnings releases and forecasts from the big AI players in the coming weeks may ease those concerns. But the bar is high – very high. Analysts expect S&P 500 earnings to rise more than 30% year-over-year for the third quarter, with two-thirds of that coming from tech and AI, according to Tajinder Dhillon, LSEG's head of earnings and equity research. Some analysts say up to 80% of the anticipated increase in total profit growth from S&P 500 companies will come from this one area. Investors are right to be cautious. On Friday, Australia's [USN:P8N42P0IJ TEXT:"Firmus"], a data center operator backed by Nvidia (NVDA.O) , shelved its $5 billion IPO. It would have been the country's second-largest initial share sale ever, and the fourth largest globally this year. That was obviously a negative twist, but even positive news from AI firms may not be good enough. On Thursday, South Korea's [USN:P8N44T045 TEXT:"Samsung"] (005930.KS) , the world's largest memory chipmaker, said it expects to announce third-quarter earnings of around $80 billion, which would be a record quarterly profit for any tech company. On the same day, Taiwan's [USN:P8N3NB03R TEXT:"TSMC "] (2330.TW) , the world's largest contract chipmaker, reported record third-quarter revenue of $46.7 billion, beating forecasts and rising 50% from a year earlier. Yet shares in both companies fell. Of course, isolated share price moves and company-specific announcements aren't indicative of the trajectory of a multi-trillion-dollar industry. But they are part of a steady drip of less-than-stellar headlines. Let's not forget, it also emerged last week that [USN:L4N45U1QQ TEXT:"OpenAI's annualized revenue"] for September was around $50 billion, down $20 billion from previous indications. This all suggests the bigger AI picture could face some seriously harsh scrutiny this earnings season. THE HIGHEST BAR The sums being spent on the AI revolution, and therefore those required to make it profitable, are eye-watering. The total cost of financing the AI buildout from last year to 2032 is estimated at $10.3 trillion, or an average of 3.63% of US gross domestic product per year, according to Columbia University professor Stijn Van Nieuwerburgh . Assuming a conservative 10% return — below the 15-20% return on investment many analysts say AI investment is targeting — Van Nieuwerburgh estimates the annual revenue required "to recover the investment, replace depreciating capital, and compensate investors for the opportunity cost of capital" is around $3.55 trillion by 2032. That's more than 9% of GDP, roughly what Americans spend on motor vehicles, transport, household furnishings, clothes, and energy combined. When you consider that annual combined revenue of OpenAI and Anthropic is currently around $100 billion, total revenue would need to grow more than 80% a year through 2032 to get to the required $3.55 trillion total, Van Nieuwerburgh says. "If the economic life of IT equipment is shorter, the revenue requirement rises substantially," he said. BIGGEST MISALLOCATION EVER? AI and tech firms' profits have, so far, mostly met Wall Street’s soaring expectations. Can they continue to do so? JPMorgan Private Bank's Michael Cembalest says AI-related stocks, which he narrows down to 41 names, have accounted for 75% of S&P 500 returns, 80% of earnings growth and 90% of capital spending growth since ChatGPT launched in November 2022. That’s an extraordinarily heavy burden for so few companies. The outlooks provided by the CEOs and CFOs of these 41 firms in the coming weeks could indicate whether a market correction could be on the horizon – and just how large it could be. AI is far and away the biggest investment boom in US history. Could it also end up being the biggest misallocation of capital? (The opinions expressed here are those of the author, a columnist for Reuters) Enjoying this column? Check out Reuters Open Interest (ROI), your essential new source for global financial commentary. Follow ROI on LinkedIn, and X. And listen to the Morning Bid daily podcast on Apple, Spotify, or the Reuters app. Subscribe to hear Reuters journalists discuss the biggest news in markets and finance seven days a week.

item.title: IonQ to buy cybersecurity firm Elisity in up to $1.3 billion deal
item.description: Quantum computing company IonQ said on Monday it would buy cybersecurity firm Elisity in an all-stock deal valued at up to $1.3 billion, as it looks to expand its quantum security business.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Quantum computing company IonQ (IONQ.N) said on Monday it would buy cybersecurity firm Elisity in an all-stock deal valued at up to $1.3 billion, as it looks to expand its quantum security business. IonQ said the acquisition would provide it with expanded channels to bring its quantum offerings to both enterprise and government customers, helping them deal with current threats and prepare for attacks from future quantum computers. Elisity, founded in 2019, has more than 100 customer deployments worldwide and has doubled its revenue and customer base year-over-year, IonQ said The deal value includes up to $150 million in earn-outs tied to Elisity's performance, it added The number of IonQ shares to be issued will be calculated at a price between $33.07 and $49.61 per share "Q-Day is coming much faster than predicted," IonQ CEO Niccolo de Masi said, referring to the point when quantum computers could break widely used encryption Elisity CEO James Winebrenner will continue to lead the acquired business after the deal closes The transaction is expected to close in the fourth quarter of 2026, subject to regulatory approval IonQ completed its acquisition of [USN:L6N3YR0UH TEXT:"chipmaker"] SkyWater Technology earlier this year to bring semiconductor manufacturing in-house and boost the development of its next-generation quantum processors

item.title: US immigration authorities raid home of Democratic Trump critic Ilhan Omar
item.description: Omar wrote on social media that the US government is being weaponized to target a political enemy of the president ahead of the midterm elections.
item.dc:creator: Nolan Mccaskill, Andrew Goudsward, Doina Chiacu
item.content:encoded: US authorities conducted a predawn raid on Monday on the Washington, DC, home of Democratic US Representative Ilhan Omar of Minnesota, an outspoken critic of Donald Trump who has been the target of political insults by the Republican president, as part of an ongoing investigation, the Justice Department said. A person familiar with the investigation said it is related to alleged immigration fraud, and part of the probe concerns the Somali-born lawmaker's immigration paperwork filled out by her late father when she was a child. Omar wrote on social media that the US government is being weaponized to target a political enemy of the president. "For ten years, Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns," Omar said. "This is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation. I will not be silenced." Other Democrats accused Trump and his administration of abuse of power. Omar, 44, is seeking a fifth two-year term in the US House of Representatives in the midterm elections on November 3. In announcing the raid, a Justice Department spokesperson said: "Today in the Washington, DC area, Homeland Security Investigations executed a judicially authorized search warrant secured by the Department of Justice. This enforcement action is part of an ongoing federal investigation." Homeland Security Investigations is part of US Immigration and Customs Enforcement, or ICE. 'SOMETHING'S GONNA HAPPEN' Trump administration border czar Tom Homan told Fox Business Network that the Justice Department is leading the investigation with the Department of Homeland Security. Homan declined to address the specifics of an ongoing criminal investigation. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, a Trump appointee, said last month that "something's gonna happen" in the investigation into Omar's family's entry into the United States. "If we can prove that you shouldn't have been here in the first place, we'll deport you," Mullin told conservative podcaster Benny Johnson at the time. Monday's raid occurred a little more than three weeks before the midterms, with Trump's party seeking to retain control of Congress. Omar, a prominent progressive, represents a safe Democratic district. She won reelection in 2024 by a margin of 50 percentage points. 'DEEPLY DISTURBING' In a statement, US House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries and other members of the party's leadership in the chamber said the raid was "deeply disturbing and raises serious questions" about the weaponization of the federal government against Trump's enemies. Republicans have "relentlessly targeted" Omar, said Jeffries, joined by Representatives Katherine Clark and Pete Aguilar. Trump's "mass deportation machine has descended upon the home of a duly elected Member of Congress and her family," they added, and they vowed to "deliver full accountability" for a "rogue abuse of power." Minnesota Democrats also condemned the raid. "Americans see this for what it is," Minnesota Governor Tim Walz wrote on social media. "President Trump is abusing his power to go after political opponents weeks before an election." Few Republican lawmakers publicly commented. One who did, Representative Nancy Mace, wrote online: "If the fraud is proven, she should be denaturalized and removed from this country. NO ONE is above the law." Justice Department policy bars federal prosecutors and agents from timing any action to affect an election's outcome or benefit a candidate or party. It historically has avoided taking investigative steps against political candidates within about 60 days of an election. George Washington University law professor Randall Eliason, a former US public corruption prosecutor, said the raid appears to be a break with past Justice Department practice of avoiding investigative steps likely to become public close to Election Day. But Eliason noted there is no way of enforcing the policy. "The idea is to avoid even the appearance of any kind of interference by the Department of Justice with the political process," Eliason said. "It's not surprising that they wouldn't really care about violating this policy because they've shown they don't really care about politicizing the Justice Department in many other ways." A person familiar with the investigation said the Justice Department consulted with its Public Integrity Section, a unit that has historically advised and approved investigations of members of Congress, and acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter prior to the search. The Trump administration has reduced the Public Integrity Section to about two lawyers and curtailed much of its authority. INVESTIGATIONS OF TRUMP CRITICS The Justice Department during Trump's second term in office has investigated and brought charges against a range of Trump's perceived political enemies. It has charged former FBI Director James Comey, New York state Attorney General Letitia James and Trump's former national security adviser turned critic John Bolton. It also has investigated Democratic lawmakers who urged the US military not to follow illegal orders, Democratic Senator Adam Schiff and Federal Reserve officials Jerome Powell and Lisa Cook. The case against James and one of two brought against Comey were thrown out by a federal judge. Bolton pleaded guilty and is scheduled to be sentenced this month. Grand juries and federal judges have stymied several other probes. 'CREEPY OBSESSION' Omar has faced political insults from Trump, who has [USN:L1N45U12W TEXT:"cast"] the Somali American community as a threat to Minnesota in a burst of anti-Somali and anti-Muslim rhetoric. Omar has called Trump's focus on her an "unhealthy and creepy obsession." Civil rights advocates have criticized Trump's rhetoric toward minorities and immigrants, including when he previously called Somalis "garbage." Trump in February said Omar and Democratic Representative Rashida Tlaib, who also is Muslim, should be "institutionalized" and sent back to "where they came from." Both lawmakers criticized Trump during his State of the Union address as he touted his administration's immigration crackdown and enforcement actions. Omar has said she and her family have faced death threats, which she attributes to "hateful political rhetoric," especially from Trump. Last month, a Minnesota man who squirted vinegar on Omar [USN:L6N4591B6 TEXT:"was sentenced"] to 14 months in prison after pleading guilty to assaulting a federal official. Anthony James Kazmierczak admitted to attacking Omar because he disagreed with her progressive views.

item.title: Dólar opera en máximos 18 meses ante escalada Oriente Medio, mercado espera dato inflación EEUU
item.description: El dólar cotizó el lunes en un máximo de 18 meses, respaldado por la demanda de activos seguros ya que una escalada del conflicto en Oriente Medio mantuvo a los inversores cautos previo a datos de inflación en Estados Unidos que se publicarán más adelante esta semana.
item.dc:creator: Laura Matthews
item.content:encoded: El dólar cotizó el lunes en un máximo de 18 meses, respaldado por la demanda de activos seguros ya que una escalada del conflicto en Oriente Medio mantuvo a los inversores cautos previo a datos de inflación en Estados Unidos que se publicarán más adelante esta semana. * El índice dólar , que mide la evolución de la moneda estadounidense frente a otras seis divisas, subía un 0,4% a 102,58 unidades, un pico desde abril de 2025. * Los precios del petróleo cotizaron con volatilidad después de que los hutíes de Yemen, respaldados por Irán, intensificaron sus ataques contra Arabia Saudita y de que dos petroleros fueron atacados durante el fin de semana. * Los futuros del crudo Brent subieron 1,93 dólares, a 106,65 dólares por barril, cerca de máximos de dos semanas, ya que los ataques eclipsaron el anuncio del domingo del presidente de Estados Unidos, Donald Trump, sobre un alto el fuego energético entre Ucrania y Rusia. * El precio de los futuros sigue estando casi un 45% por encima del nivel que tenía antes de que comenzara la guerra entre Estados Unidos e Israel contra Irán. * La presidenta de la Reserva Federal de Cleveland, Beth Hammack, dijo el lunes que el banco central de Estados Unidos debería adoptar "con relativa rapidez" una postura de política monetaria restrictiva para controlar una inflación que, en su opinión, se ha generalizado y está empezando a influir en los planes de fijación de precios de las empresas. * Los datos semanales del regulador de los mercados estadounidenses muestran que los inversionistas han ido aumentando sus posiciones alcistas en el dólar, que ascendieron a unos 36.000 millones de dólares en la semana que finalizó el 7 de octubre, frente a los apenas 8.400 millones de dólares de hace tres semanas , en gran parte a costa del euro. * El reporte sobre la inflación al consumidor de Estados Unidos del miércoles, una de las últimas publicaciones económicas importantes antes de la reunión de política monetaria de la Reserva Federal de este mes, podría ser clave para determinar la dirección a corto plazo del dólar. * Los datos de la semana pasada mostraron que la confianza de los consumidores estadounidenses se deterioró aún más a principios de octubre, ya que el aumento del costo de la vida debido al conflicto en Oriente Medio empañó la visión que tienen los hogares de la economía. * La Fed subió las tasas el mes pasado por primera vez desde 2023 para frenar la inflación, y los mercados siguen de cerca los datos económicos para evaluar si los responsables de política monetaria podrían volver a actuar. * Los operadores descuentan una probabilidad del 78% de que la Fed mantenga las tasas sin cambios este mes, frente al 51% del mes anterior, según la herramienta FedWatch de CME. * El euro caía un 0,4% a 1,1156 dólares, cerca de un piso de 17 meses, tras registrar la semana pasada su quinta semana consecutiva de pérdidas, debido a la inquietud de los inversionistas en torno a la salud fiscal de Francia de cara a las elecciones presidenciales de 2027. * Frente al yen , el dólar subía un 0,2% a 158,57 yenes, en una sesión con escaso volumen de operaciones en Japón debido a un festivo, mientras que la libra caía un 0,2% a 1,3203 dólares.

item.title: UN refugee agency's funding shortfall is impacting refugees worldwide, its chief says
item.description: GENEVA: Deep funding shortfalls are forcing the UN refugee agency to make painful cuts across its humanitarian operations worldwide, and there are limits to how much restructuring can offset shrinking donor support, its chief said on Monday (Oct 12).UNHCR has secured only US$3 billion, or 35 per cent of the U
item.dc:creator: CNA
item.content:encoded:

UN refugee agency's funding shortfall is impacting refugees worldwide, its chief says

United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) Barham Salih addresses the United Nations Security Council, at the UN headquarters in New York City on Sep 25, 2026. (File Photo: Reuters/Jeenah Moon)

FAST

GENEVA: Deep funding shortfalls are forcing the UN refugee agency to make painful cuts across its humanitarian operations worldwide, and there are limits to how much restructuring can offset shrinking donor support, its chief said on Monday (Oct 12). UNHCR has secured only US$3 billion, or 35 per cent of the US$8.5 billion in funding it requires for 2026, High Commissioner Barham Salih told the agency's executive committee at a meeting in Geneva. The shortfall follows aid cuts by countries including the United States under President Donald Trump at a time of record global displacement. Funding for next year remains uncertain although the expected figure of around $2.68 billion could improve after a UNHCR donor pledging conference in December, Salih said.

UNHCR has launched one of its largest restructurings in the agency's history because of the budget squeeze, with Salih saying its workforce had been reduced since 2024 from 20,000 employees to just under 12,000. "Protection has a floor. Below it, the system does not simply become smaller. The protection we can provide begins to fail," he said. Salih cautioned that restructuring could not compensate indefinitely for lower funding, and that the funding crisis was already having tangible consequences for refugees and humanitarian partners. "There is a difference between doing more with less and being asked to do the impossible," he said.

Related:

IN FOCUS: 'I cannot go back' - Myanmar refugees fear repatriation as country gets cosier with Malaysia, Thailand

Number of forcibly displaced people dips to 118 million: UN

JOB CUTS UNHCR is seeking to preserve frontline operations by cutting jobs at its Geneva headquarters and worldwide regional offices, with 88 per cent of staff remaining outside headquarters, Salih said. About 95 per cent of the staff doing protection work, such as registering refugees and providing legal assistance, and helping refugees find longer-term solutions, such as returning home safely, have been retained in field locations, he said.  He cited several examples of programmes under threat.  In Chad, he said, insufficient funding risks disrupting specialised medical care and legal assistance for more than 50,000 survivors of conflict-related sexual violence who fled neighbouring Sudan.  In Ethiopia, refugee registration had been suspended for tens of thousands of refugees from South Sudan and Eritrea, he said. Colombia has raised concerns on behalf of Latin American countries that their region is being disproportionately impacted.  The Americas, which include the US, Canada, Latin America and the Caribbean, face a budget reduction of 32 per cent in 2027 compared to this year, or about $485 million — the largest budget reduction of any region — while the number of forcibly displaced and stateless people in the Americas is projected to increase by 4 per cent to about 24.5 million people in 2027, Salih said.

Source: Reuters/ia

item.title: ＥＵのＨＶ輸入上限枠、中国ＥＶ各社に打撃 欧州現地生産加速へ
item.description: ［上海／北京 １２日 ロイター］ - 中国が欧州連合（ＥＵ）向けのハイブリッド車（ＨＶ）輸出を抑えることに同意した。国内...
item.dc:creator: ロイター
item.content:encoded:
ＥＵのＨＶ輸入上限枠、中国ＥＶ各社に打撃　欧州現地生産加速へ 10/12 20:33 配信

2026年4月15日、南アフリカ・ヨハネスブルグでのイベントで撮影　REUTERS/Nqobile Dludla/File Photo

［上海／北京　１２日　ロイター］ - 中国が欧州連合（ＥＵ）向けのハイブリッド車（ＨＶ）輸出を抑えることに同意した。国内販売の伸びが鈍る中、中国の電気自動車（ＥＶ）メーカーにとって新たな打撃になる。

中国商務省は１２日、この取り決めで輸出は今後も増やせるとし、中国には他のどの輸入元に割り当てられる枠よりも小さくない数量枠が保証されると表明した。

中国自動車各社は、ＥＵの中国製ＥＶに課す関税の対象外であるＨＶの輸出を増やしてきた。中国税関のデータによると、２０２６年上半期のＥＵ向けＨＶ輸出額は７５億ドルと、前年同期（２５億ドル）の３倍だった。

ジェフリーズによると、上海汽車集団（ＳＡＩＣ）、比亜迪（ＢＹＤ）、奇瑞汽車の３社が、ＥＵで販売される中国製ＨＶの９割超（台数ベース）を占める。３社の欧州販売では、半分以上がＨＶとなっている。

シュミット・オートモーティブ・リサーチによると、欧州ＥＶ市場での中国ブランドのシェアは２６年第２・四半期に過去最高の１５％となった。２４年第１・四半期は９．５％だった。ＰＨＥＶ市場でも中国製のシェアは４分の１を超え、２４年初めのわずか１．７％から急拡大した。

＜現地生産加速へ＞

仏ルノーのフランソワ・プロボ最高経営責任者（ＣＥＯ）は１２日、中国製ＨＶの輸入急増は欧州にとって持続可能ではないと述べた。一方で、今回の合意は貿易戦争よりは望ましいとし、通商関係を「賢明に」管理する必要があると指摘した。

投資家はおおむね、今回の合意を貿易摩擦の緩和と受け止め、中国製ＨＶへの関税が当面は見送られる兆しとみている。

シティのアナリストは、実施ルール、数量上限、最低価格などは、今後さらなる協議が必要だが、とりあえずリスクが緩和したと指摘した。

中国の自動車業界に詳しいコンサルタントのマイケル・ダン氏は「中国が合意を守るのか、それとも抜け道や一時的な関税免除を見つけるのか、見ていきたい」と述べた。

アナリストらは、数量枠の制度が始まる前に輸出を前倒しする動きが出る可能性があるが、合意は最終的に、中国の自動車メーカーによる欧州での現地生産を加速させる可能性があるとみる。

上海のコンサルティング会社オートモビリティの創業者、ビル・ルッソ氏は「これで、中国の自動車メーカーが欧州で生産する動機は強まるだろう」と述べた。

ロイター 関連ニュース コラム：ＥＵのＥＶ補助金巡る対中調査、自らに跳ね返るリスクも コラム：短距離フライト削減でＣＯ2対策なるか、的外れの欧州 焦点：トランプ政権の影で歩み寄るカナダとＥＵ、準加盟提示でも見える限界 焦点：コーヒー企業「アフリカ離れ」も、ＥＵが森林破壊防止法 アングル：長時間労働・残業に不満の中国労働者、ＥＵの対中圧力に「共感」 最終更新: 10/12(月) 20:33 ロイター

Surfing hotspots around the world are more vulnerable to climate change, says new study

The research analysed 57 surf breaks across eight countries to arrive at its findings. Each of the sites selected is incorporated into a World Surfing Reserve.

Purvi Rajpuria

12 October, 2026 04:43 pm IST

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

Linkedin

Representative image (c) Copyright Thomson Reuters 2024

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

New Delhi: Many of the most prominent surf breaks across the world are vulnerable to climate change, even as the degree and type of vulnerability differ widely, a recent study found.

The study, titled ‘ Globally significant surf breaks are vulnerable to climate change ’, was co-authored by Dan R Reineman of California State University Channel Islands, along with researchers from Save The Waves Coalition and World Surfing Reserves .

The research analysed 57 surf breaks across eight countries to arrive at its findings. Each of the sites selected is incorporated into a World Surfing Reserve (WSR)—“a status applied for by local stakeholders and designated by an international non-profit organization based on each site’s cultural, historical, and environmental significance for surfing,” the study explains.

Show Full Article

These surf breaks, the research found, are vulnerable to climate change, due to changing tide levels, hardened shorelines caused by manmade structures, and shifting sands. Surf breaks rated at most risk include Croyde beach in north Devon, UK, and Oriente Salvaje in El Salvador.

What are surf breaks? Dan Reineman, a co-author of the study, pointed to the several factors that come together to form a surf break. “Surf breaks are incredibly unique oceanographic phenomena – a confluence of all these factors that fit together just right to make the wave happen – and so those processes are really sensitive,” he said .

Some of these factors include swell direction, tide, and intricate combinations of sea-floor shape. Climate change, global warming, and changing rainfall patterns can affect any of these factors, hampering the delicate balance of surf breaks and thus destroying the wave.

Significantly, the study found that coastlines that were more natural and less populated by manmade structures could adapt better to the changes caused by climate change. These coastlines were able to adapt by shifting inland and relocating sediments. Construction of features such as sea walls, jetties and groynes made the beaches and waves less resilient, Reineman said .

Also read: Mamdani has a new target. Subscriptions that make cancellations difficult

Affects local economy at large Climate change-related vulnerability matters not only to surfers, but also to the local people who depend on the multi-billion-dollar surf economy that exists in these sites.

Adam Hall, a co-founder of the North Devon WSR, was one of the local surfers who contributed to the study. Explaining the significance of surfing to the local economy, he said , “Surfers will come throughout the year. They fill up the pubs, restaurants and car parks when the swells are good in January, February and March, where if you go to any other tourist destination that doesn’t have surf, they’re dead on their knees.”

Many of these sites often have little else in terms of local economy.

Local surfers also played a key role in guiding the research. Trent Hodges, a co-author of the study and a senior programmes manager at Save the Waves Coalition, said , “We learned directly from the local surfers how they are seeing their waves change. It’s a canary in the coalmine too – when a wave changes, that often means the beach is changing, and everybody enjoys the beach.”

The study also hypothesises that similar risks could affect other surf breaks, not included in the present research, and encourages other local people and organisations to assess their vulnerability.

(Edited by Ratan Priya)

FAST

Oct 12 : Norway's data protection authority has fined Microsoft's adtech unit Xandr 92 million crowns ($9.61 million) for unlawfully relaying Grindr users' sensitive data to thousands of advertisers, it said on Monday. Xandr relayed data revealing the sexual orientation of users of Grindr, a dating app for LGBTQIA+ people, to companies in automated ad auctions from July 2018 to April 2020. It is the biggest fine the Norwegian authority has issued, and targets the advertising middlemen rather than the app itself. The regulator said companies that traded in people's data could not pass the blame to others. The data protection authority fined Grindr 65 million crowns over the same breaches in 2021.

The fine was based on Xandr's revenue, not Microsoft's, which did not own the unit at the time. Xandr has three weeks to appeal. Xandr said it assumed Grindr had obtained users' consent and never checked, the data protection authority said. It rejected that argument and ruled Xandr shared legal responsibility with Grindr.  Microsoft said the privacy of users was a top priority. "This investigation and decision focused on conduct that predates Microsoft's acquisition of Xandr, and in that time the interpretation and application of legal standards and practices has continued to evolve. We are reviewing the decision and assessing our options," it said. The case began with a 2020 complaint by the Norwegian Consumer Council, whose research exposed how apps shared user data, and Austrian data privacy organisation noyb, which called the decision "a valuable precedent".   ($1 = 9.5704 Norwegian crowns)

Source: Reuters

item.title: Crudo sube tras los ataques a Arabia Saudita, lo que eclipsa el acuerdo de Trump sobre diésel
item.description: Los precios del petróleo subieron casi 2 dólares por barril el lunes, ya que los ataques contra Arabia Saudita pesaron más que la perspectiva de un aumento de la oferta, a pesar de que el presidente de Estados Unidos, Donald Trump, celebró las nuevas exportaciones rusas de diésel y el alto el fuego entre Rusia y Ucrania en materia de objetivos energéticos.
item.dc:creator: Shadia Nasralla
item.content:encoded: Los precios del petróleo subieron casi 2 dólares por barril el lunes, ya que los ataques contra Arabia Saudita pesaron más que la perspectiva de un aumento de la oferta, a pesar de que el presidente de Estados Unidos, Donald Trump, celebró las nuevas exportaciones rusas de diésel y el alto el fuego entre Rusia y Ucrania en materia de objetivos energéticos. *Los futuros del crudo Brent cerraron con una subida de 1,93 dólares, o un 1,8 %, hasta los 106,65 dólares por barril, su nivel más alto desde el 15 de septiembre. El crudo West Texas Intermediate (WTI) de Estados Unidos cerró en 93,74 dólares por barril, con una subida de 1,89 dólares, o un 2 %. *Los hutíes, alineados con Irán, reivindicaron la autoría de un ataque perpetrado el sábado contra el aeropuerto internacional de Riad, en el que murieron 13 personas y más de 300 resultaron heridas. El domingo se produjeron nuevos ataques, lo que intensificó un conflicto que podría obstaculizar aún más el suministro de crudo procedente de uno de los mayores productores del mundo. *"El impactante ataque con misiles de los hutíes contra el aeropuerto de Riad, en Arabia Saudita, provocará, obviamente, una escalada de las represalias contra los hutíes en Yemen", afirmó el inversor y analista Louis Navellier en una nota. "En estos momentos, las refinerías de Arabia Saudita están en funcionamiento, pero cinco de ellas se cerraron temporalmente cuando se interrumpió un oleoducto hacia el mar Rojo tras los ataques con misiles". *Este mes se han registrado más ataques contra petroleros que navegaban por el estrecho de Ormuz, lo que amenaza con frenar la recuperación de las exportaciones de crudo de Oriente Medio observada en septiembre. *Un petrolero fue alcanzado por un dron en las proximidades de Sohar, en Omán, mientras que otro sufrió daños al transitar por el estrecho de Ormuz, según informó la Agencia de Operaciones de Comercio Marítimo del Reino Unido. *"La sensación de cierta normalidad en las exportaciones desde el estrecho de Ormuz se hizo añicos la semana pasada. Los nuevos ataques de los hutíes contra Arabia Saudita se sumaron a ello y contribuyeron a la subida de los precios", afirmó Bjarne Schieldrop, analista de materias primas de SEB. *"Cada vez habrá que tomar decisiones más difíciles sobre qué defender: la infraestructura petrolera, las instalaciones militares, los palacios reales, los aeropuertos civiles u otros". *Goldman Sachs, en una nota, elevó su previsión del precio del Brent para diciembre de 85 a 90 dólares por barril, estimando una prima de riesgo de algo más de 20 dólares por barril. *Los precios del WTI, añadieron, probablemente se mantendrían bajos frente al Brent debido a los elevados costos de transporte entre Estados Unidos y Europa, y se situarían en una media de 81 dólares en diciembre de 2026 y de 73 dólares en 2027. *En el Golfo de México, las grandes empresas energéticas Shell (SHEL.L) , Chevron (CVX.N) y BP intentaban reubicar a su personal y restablecer la producción en sus plataformas después de que el huracán Isaías tocara tierra la madrugada del sábado.

item.title: Nasdaq falls ahead of earnings, economic data while oil rallies
item.description: The technology-heavy Nasdaq composite closed lower on Monday as oil prices jumped nearly $2 a barrel after attacks on a Saudi airport, and investors waited for banks to kick off the third-quarter earnings season and for economic data this week.
item.dc:creator: Sinead Carew, Ragini Mathur
item.content:encoded: The technology-heavy Nasdaq composite closed lower on Monday as oil prices jumped nearly $2 a barrel after attacks on a Saudi airport, and investors waited for banks to kick off the third-quarter earnings season and for economic data this week. The S&P 500 ended the session barely lower while the Dow advanced. Oil futures rallied after deadly [USN:L1N45X01E TEXT:"strikes on Riyadh's international airport"] over the weekend. The attacks overshadowed the prospect of increased supplies after US President [USN:L1N45X021 TEXT:"Donald Trump"] hailed fresh Russian diesel exports and talked about a Russia-Ukraine ceasefire on energy targets. In coming days, US investors will focus on corporate earnings, with major US banks including Goldman Sachs (GS.N) , Citigroup (C.N) and JPMorgan Chase (JPM.N) reporting early on Tuesday. Analysts were expecting S&P 500 earnings to surge 30.6% in the third quarter, according to LSEG IBES data. Also due out this week are September readings for US consumer and producer inflation as well as retail sales data. While the US Treasury market was closed on Monday for Columbus Day, stock investors have been wary of bond yields' recent advance to [USN:L8N45T173 TEXT:"24-year highs"] as elevated energy prices have stoked inflation concerns. "Looking out further in the week, we have some big economic reports," said Tim Ghriskey, senior portfolio strategist at Ingalls & Snyder in New York. He said investors were also cautious due to a lack of direction from bonds. "We're also waiting on earnings and that's significant. The four large banks reporting on Tuesday can have a big impact," he said. The Dow Jones Industrial Average (.DJI) rose 195.60 points, or 0.38%, to 51,850.55, the S&P 500 (.SPX) lost 4.30 points, or 0.06%, to 7,807.24 and the Nasdaq Composite (.IXIC) lost 120.27 points, or 0.44%, to 27,245.90. Trading volume was relatively light with 12.67 billion shares changing hands on US exchanges compared with the 20-day moving average of 17.62 billion. "There's a lot to be wary of," said Robert Pavlik, senior portfolio manager at Dakota Wealth in Fairfield, Connecticut, pointing to upcoming data and earnings along with rising oil prices. "You're walking down a train line and you don't know, because it's dark, if a train is coming and so, you know, you're just being real careful," he said. With oil prices rising, energy (.SPNY) outperformed among the S&P 500's 11 major industry sectors with a 1.5% advance. The defensive consumer staples sector (.SPLRCS) rose more than 1% along with the S&P 500 communication services index (.SPLRCL) , which was boosted by a more than 3% gain in heavyweight Meta (META.O) . Technology (.SPLRCT) , down 0.9%, and consumer discretionary (.SPLRCD) , off 0.7%, were the biggest sector laggards. Technology's weakness was most pronounced among chip stocks with the Philadelphia semiconductor index (.SOX) finishing down 2.7% after hitting a three-week low. In consumer discretionary, Chipotle Mexican Grill (CMG.N) shares fell 3.8% after Starbucks (SBUX.O) said [USN:L4N45Y0TM TEXT:"it was not buying"] the burrito chain. Starbucks shares closed up 1.7%. Microsoft (MSFT.O) finished up 1.1% with its market capitalization climbing above $4 trillion for the first time in a year after it [USN:L6N45V11Z TEXT:"announced plans for major deployment"] of its own AI chips. Salesforce (CRM.N) shares added 2% after BofA Global Research upgraded the stock to "buy" from "underperform." Also eBay (EBAY.O) rose 2% after Morgan Stanley added the stock to its top-pick list. Meanwhile, Cleveland Federal Reserve President [USN:S0N44V02D TEXT:"Beth Hammack"] said the US central bank should move "relatively quickly" to a more restrictive monetary policy stance to fight inflation, which she feels has become more broad-based and is starting to influence firms' price-setting plans. Traders were pricing in an almost 22% chance the US Federal Reserve will hike interest rates this month, according to CME's FedWatch tool, up from 17.7% on Friday. Declining issues outnumbered advancers by a 1.09-to-1 ratio on the NYSE where there were 149 new highs and 272 new lows. On the Nasdaq, 1,888 stocks rose and 3,008 fell as declining issues outnumbered advancers by a 1.59-to-1 ratio. The S&P 500 posted 10 new 52-week highs and five new lows while the Nasdaq Composite recorded 51 new highs and 318 new lows.

item.title: ノーベル経済学賞、米大教授2人に 経済安定化の研究
item.description: ［ストックホルム １２日 ロイター］ -
item.dc:creator: ロイター
item.content:encoded:
［ストックホルム　１２日　ロイター］ - スウェーデン王立科学アカデミーは１２日、２０２６年のノーベル経済学賞を米スタンフォード大学のロバート・ホール教授（８３）と米コロンビア大学のマイケル・ウッドフォード教授（７０）に授与すると発表した。授賞理由は「マクロ経済の安定化に関するミクロ経済学的基盤」。

両氏は、効果的な安定化政策を実行する能力を向上させる新たなボトムアップ型の経済モデルを開発した。これにより、経済に打撃を与える変動の激しさを緩和できる、適切なタイミングでの財政・金融政策の実施が可能となり、世界の中央銀行や財務省で活用されている。

経済学賞選考委員会のジョン・ハスラー委員長は声明で「両氏の功績は、現在世界中の各中央銀行や政府によって使われているモデルに安定した理論的基盤を提供した」と指摘。「両氏のモデルによって、エネルギー危機や家計消費の急変動など、経済へのショックにより適切に対処できるようになった」と述べた。

両氏の重要な洞察の一つは、経済の仕組みを上から捉えるトップダウン型の理論に頼るのではなく、家計や企業がミクロのレベルで下す無数の決定を考慮して初めて経済を安定させられるという点だ。

ウッドフォード氏は会見で「当局は、経済の安定化を、経済の中にいる人々がそれをどう理解しているかとは関係なく、誰かがレバーを引いて経済を操作するだけの作業と見なすべきではない」と語った。

ウッドフォード氏によると、中銀が高騰するインフレへの対応に苦しんだ１９７０年代の石油危機とは違い、２０００年代後半の世界金融危機では、新たな枠組みが伝統的な金融政策手段を補う上で役に立った。

「すぐに追加利下げできることだけに頼るのではなく、金利政策が今後どうなりそうかをより明確に表明することが、０９年以降の政策対応の重要な部分を占めた」と述べた。

両氏の研究は、金融政策の先行きを示す、いわゆる「フォワードガイダンス」のほかにも、需要が変化しても価格の変化が遅れる「粘着的な」インフレ、「需給ギャップ（アウトプットギャップ）」といった現在使われている概念を広めた。

item.title: Most Americans oppose betting on elections, government events, Reuters/Ipsos poll finds
item.description: Most Americans oppose using prediction markets to bet on US elections and other government actions, according to a Reuters/Ipsos opinion poll that suggests the booming markets may lack broad public support as policymakers debate how to regulate them.
item.dc:creator: Chris Prentice, Jason Lange
item.content:encoded: Most Americans oppose using prediction markets to bet on US elections and other government actions, according to a Reuters/Ipsos opinion poll that suggests the booming markets may lack broad public support as policymakers debate how to regulate them. The [USN:L4N42Y0WQ TEXT:"rapidly growing prediction market industry"] led by Polymarket and Kalshi allows people to bet on a raft of events, including US elections, government policy moves and sports games, raising concerns among policymakers that the platforms are opening up new avenues for [USN:L6N44E0TQ TEXT:"insider trading"] and manipulation. The companies say they have [USN:L4N42H1L3 TEXT:"extensive controls"] to guard against misconduct, that their markets are often better at forecasting outcomes than traditional polls, and that they [USN:L6N44L0X4 TEXT:"offer unique ways to hedge"] a range of esoteric real-world risks. Yet a bipartisan majority of Americans is opposed to using prediction markets to bet on US elections , military actions and government policy announcements or decisions, according to the Reuters/Ipsos poll conducted September 30 through October 5. Some 69% of Democrats and 61% of Republicans said they opposed using prediction markets to bet on election results. Sixty-five percent of Americans opposed prediction market betting on US military actions and 63% opposed betting on government policy announcements or decisions, suggesting broad bipartisan discomfort with wagering on government affairs. Only 8% and 9%, respectively, supported such bets. The results shed more light on popular attitudes toward the nascent industry, which is marketing heavily on social media and TV even as it faces pushback from states and from Democratic lawmakers who argue the markets are unethical, socially corrosive and could undermine national security. "Everyone should make their own decisions about their lives," said Ronna Schmoker, 72, a Democrat from a Dallas suburb who participated in the poll. "But like anything, you have to have guardrails." A Polymarket spokesperson said Americans are bombarded with misinformation from various sources, and that prediction markets help provide unbiased, accurate information. "It’s why more than 90% of visits to Polymarket are to view markets, not to trade," the spokesperson said. "Recognition of the public value of prediction markets is growing, but they’re still brand new to most, and it’s going to take some time for the public to learn more and see the real value." NATIONAL SECURITY AND ELECTION FEARS HAVE STOKED DEBATE Some policymakers worry that prediction markets, which offer thousands of ways to wager on the US midterms, [USN:L6N41V1AT TEXT:"could undermine faith in"] the integrity of US democracy and enable government insiders to broadcast confidential information via their trades. Reuters reported [USN:L6N44E0TQ TEXT:"in August"] that more than 150 accounts on Polymarket International, the company's overseas market which bars US users, may have traded on inside military information, while Kalshi [USN:L1N41514R TEXT:"has suspended candidates"] for betting on their own races. Kalshi banned former Republican Representative George Santos, who agreed to pay $35,000 [USN:L6N43X19K TEXT:"to resolve government allegations"] of manipulative trading after he bet via Kalshi on whether he would attend the State of the Union address. Santos did not admit to the allegations and said through his attorney that he never intended to deceive anyone. Ninety-three percent of Democrats and 89% of Republicans said it was inappropriate for members of Congress or their staff to bet on political events, while 6% and 8%, respectively, said it was appropriate. Polymarket and Kalshi say they work closely with the authorities and routinely refer suspicious accounts, and have introduced various restrictions to mitigate misconduct. Kalshi says it does not allow trading on military operations and bars political candidates from wagering on their own races. The Senate in April barred senators, staff and other officers from using prediction markets, and [USN:L4N4051K3 TEXT:"several Democratic lawmakers have introduced bills"] to restrict the industry. "We see prediction markets everywhere, but don't mistake seeing millions of dollars in advertisements as a sign of growing support," said Democratic Senator Jeff Merkley of Oregon. "Folks are rightfully concerned." The Reuters/Ipsos poll suggests many Americans are generally uneasy about increasingly commoditizing real-world events. Even betting on professional sports, a far more established activity, was opposed by 43% of respondents, while 29% supported it. "I just don't think it's good for a society to bet on whether things will turn out a certain way," said Michael Clark, a 48-year-old conservative who lives outside Dallas and participated in the poll. TRUMP ADMINISTRATION HAS SUPPORTED INDUSTRY GROWTH The administration of President Donald Trump, whose son Donald Trump Jr. has business ties to Kalshi and Polymarket, is pursuing federal regulations for the industry, a move states are fighting. Legal experts expect that dispute to reach the Supreme Court. At issue is whether prediction markets facilitate trading in financial instruments or gambling, which is regulated by the states. State regulators say they are facilitating gambling and should be subject to more stringent state laws, while Trump's Commodity Futures Trading Commission has asserted jurisdiction, arguing the contracts are a type of financial product it regulates. "By that rationale, MGM (Resorts) owns dozens of financial markets," said Glenn Rishton, a 76-year-old Republican poll respondent in Gulfport, Mississippi, referring to the casino company. "It's effectively gambling." Three-quarters of Americans agreed, with only 8% saying using prediction markets to wager on the outcome of real-world events is not a form of gambling. A spokesperson for the Coalition for Prediction Markets said its research found that Republican and Democratic voters alike prefer a federal regulatory framework over a patchwork of state rules. The Reuters/Ipsos poll, which was conducted online and nationwide, surveyed 4,506 US adults and had a margin of error of about two percentage points. "Prediction markets should have the same level of regulations as gambling," said Janessa Manning, 48, a Democrat in Detroit. "Even though they pretend they aren’t gambling, they are."

item.title: Citi seeks rapid resolution of its US regulatory burdens
item.description: Citigroup is seeking to rapidly resolve its efforts to address regulatory demands that have long dogged the third-largest US bank, in order to fully re-focus on growth, according to two people familiar with the matter.
item.dc:creator: Tatiana Bautzer, Nupur Anand
item.content:encoded: Citigroup (C.N) is seeking to rapidly resolve its efforts to address [USN:L6N3YV14X TEXT:"regulatory demands"] that have long dogged the third-largest US bank, in order to fully re-focus on growth, according to two people familiar with the matter. The demands have lingered since 2020, leading to costly fines and distractions for Citi. As recently as the summer, Citi was targeting submitting paperwork to regulators before the end of the year, or during the first quarter, one of the people told Reuters. The bank has been aiming to present a comprehensive audit to the Federal Reserve and Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, so it will not hit any delays in approval, the person said. It will then wind down part of its remediation structure, the two sources said. This would finally set the bank on a path to have consent orders lifted. The orders cover the regulatory [USN:L6N3YV14X TEXT:"demands to fix "]risk management, data governance and other problems. Investors and analysts are laser focused on when Citi might shake off its regulatory burden, which could free up resources, boost the stock and become a key achievement for Chief Executive Jane Fraser. Fraser has said Citi is about 90% done with the regulatory work required under the orders. SPEEDING UP Wells Fargo analyst Mike Mayo said an exit "would be seen as a validation of their restructuring process, and Citigroup shares may then attract a larger group of investors". Earlier this year, Reuters reported that the bank had hoped to finish the job by the end of 2026. While Citi has never acknowledged an official timeline, the person familiar with the matter said that it is under pressure to achieve this as soon as possible, but ran into a brief audit-related delay over the summer. Citi did not comment on any motivation for getting out of the consent orders as soon as possible, but said such a decision rested with regulators. "The way Citi is run today is fundamentally different from where we started our Transformation, and we are committed to ensuring the changes we have been making to strengthen our risk and control environment are sustainable," a Citi spokesman said. "As we have said consistently, we will not speculate about the lifting of the consent orders because that remains solely at our regulators’ discretion," the spokesman added. AREAS OF PROMISE Citi's regulatory [USN:L6N3XN1GA TEXT:"distractions"] have come at a time when rivals have taken advantage of the government's lighter-touch banking policies, including over supervision and rules, analysts say. Filings show the bank spent $3.3 billion on "transformation" work last year. It is set to [USN:L1N45R0GT TEXT:"report its earnings on Tuesday"]. In a research report, Bank of America analyst Ebrahim Poonawala said Citi's wealth division "shows the greatest room for improvement" among its five core franchises, for which it needs to accelerate growth of investment assets, and tilt revenues toward fee income and away from spread income. The division still has the lowest return of all five businesses, at 12.6% in the first half of the year, with a long term goal of 20%. The two people familiar with the matter said the wealth management and retail businesses could benefit from increased scale, with one potential solution being to add branches or acquire a wealth manager. While such moves to expand are not formally prohibited under the consent orders, they are more closely scrutinized by regulators, reinforcing the need to quickly address their demands. "It is tougher to focus on any relevant growth before you fix the problems," said Tim Long, a former deputy comptroller at the OCC. "It makes sense for the bank to try to get the orders finalized in this (Trump) administration and avoid potential change of regulators and a different approach." FAVORABLE POLICIES Any potential acquisition would force Citi to consider both regulators' and investors' appetite, especially after speculation of an imminent deal was [USN:L4N40F1AJ TEXT:"badly received "][USN:L4N40F1AJ TEXT:"by the market"] earlier this year. Fraser later told investors on an earnings call: "We are only interested in and focused on organic growth. Period. End of story". The Trump administration , now nearing the midpoint of its term, has so far been broadly favorable for banks, despite the president attacking some firms including [USN:L4N3YN1QS TEXT:"JPMorgan"] and [USN:S0N3OG012 TEXT:"Bank of America"]. Trump has on the other hand praised Citi in a social media post for its investment banking growth. Financial regulators under Trump have addressed several of the industry's longstanding gripes, including trimming barriers to mergers as part of the administration's overall bid to ease regulation. Some industry executives say they are wary that a future Democratic administration could reconsider these policies. DATA TRACING Citi's road to fixing past errors has been long and bumpy. It traces back to a botched $900 million transfer to Revlon creditors, which triggered a 2020 demand by the Federal Reserve and OCC to remediate longstanding risk management and data governance problems. It was fined $400 million and the bank agreed to fix the identified issues. Four years later, the OCC fined it again for a delay in addressing data and other problems related to the original consent orders and requested in an amendment that Citi come up with a plan showing the resources it would allocate to address the issues. The OCC lifted that amendment in December 2025 [USN:L4N3XO1DA TEXT:"but the original consent order was outstanding"]. One of the people who spoke to Reuters said that the bank had carefully checked remediation work to be shown to the regulator, with one internal audit in the summer rejecting a version presented on data tracing – specifically, the ability to track the origin of aggregated accounts. Making sure the internal audits are rigorous will be key to streamlining the process and avoid extensive checks on Citi's work, the person said. The lifting of the consent orders would require sign-off from the Fed and OCC. The Fed declined to comment for this article. The OCC did not respond to a request for comment.

item.title: Hall, Woodford win Nobel prize for work on how to stabilise economies
item.description: US academics Robert Hall and Michael Woodford won the 2026 Nobel economics prize on Monday for decades of work developing ground-up models currently used by central banks and finance ministries across the world to stabilise economies.
item.dc:creator: Simon Johnson, Johan Ahlander
item.content:encoded: US academics Robert Hall and Michael Woodford won the 2026 Nobel economics prize on Monday for decades of work developing ground-up models currently used by central banks and finance ministries across the world to stabilise economies. "With them, we are better equipped to deal with shocks in the economy, such as energy crises or sudden changes in how much households consume," John Hassler, Chair of the Committee for the Prize in Economic Sciences, said in a statement. Woodford and Hall are frequently name-checked by the world's [USN:L6N45A0IG TEXT:"top central banks"] which, after a 2022 inflation surge in the aftermath of the COVID-19 pandemic, are currently grappling with the energy shock triggered by the Iran war . One of the laureates' key insights is that economies could only be kept on an even keel by taking into account the millions of decisions made at a micro-level by households and businesses, rather than by using top-down theories of how economies work. "Authorities shouldn't view stabilization of the economy as an exercise that is simply conducted by people pulling levers to control the economy independently of what people in the economy understand about this," Columbia University's Woodford, 70, told a news conference. In contrast to the oil shocks of the 1970s, when central banks struggled to combat sky-high inflation, Woodford said the new framework was useful during the global financial crisis of the late-2000s to bolster traditional tools of monetary policy. "Making more explicit statements about the likely future path of interest rate policy, as opposed to relying on simply being able to cut interest rates further immediately, that was an important part of the policy response in the years from 2009 onward," he said. Beyond so-called "forward guidance" on the future path of monetary policy, the work of Woodford - and Hall, 83, at Stanford University – promoted other concepts used today such as the idea of "sticky" inflation when price changes lag changes in demand. Another is the "output gap", a measure of demand pressure building up in an economy and how efficiently resources are being used, with the goal of stabilisation policy being to steer that gap towards zero. CORE CENTRAL BANK CONCEPTS Hall has served as adviser to the US Treasury Department, the Justice Department and the Federal Reserve Board. His insight in a 1978 paper that household decisions on consumption are a perfect indicator of their expectations was used by Woodford in a model on how consumption is determined. Hall called the prize "a wonderful surprise" in a statement. "I've spent my career trying to understand how the economy works," he said. "When I thought I had a new idea, the next step was to find out whether it was actually new, whether it was right, and whether it mattered." Woodford also showed that central banks can stimulate or suppress economic activity by adjusting interest rates, rather than just by the amount of money in circulation. Such concepts remain core to [USN:L1N40L06U TEXT:"central banking today"]. Forward guidance became especially important after the 2008 financial crisis, when rates were near zero or even negative and standard monetary policy seemed to be out of ammunition. Now, however, some are questioning how relevant it is given the amount of uncertainty in the global economy – with new US Federal Reserve Chair [USN:L6N43T122 TEXT:"Kevin Warsh"] a notable sceptic. The economics prize, formally known as the Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel, is the final award to be given out this year and is worth 12 million Swedish crowns ($1.2 million). First awarded in 1969, it is not one of the original five awards created in the 1895 will of industrialist and dynamite inventor Alfred Nobel, but was established by Sweden's central bank. The majority of previous laureates have been from the United States. Only three women have ever won, most recently Claudia Goldin in 2023 for work on how gender has affected pay and employment over time in the United States. [USN:L2N3VU08K TEXT:"Last year's winners"], Joel Mokyr, Philippe Aghion and Peter Howitt, won for work on "creative destruction" and how new technology and production methods can boost growth and living standards. The Nobel prizes for [USN:L1N45R0AK TEXT:"medicine"], [USN:L1N45S0E6 TEXT:"physics"], [USN:L1N45T09K TEXT:"chemistry"], [USN:L1N45U0CQ TEXT:"literature"] and [USN:L8N45V0JG TEXT:"peace"] were announced last week. ($1 = 10.0028 Swedish crowns)

item.title: Kyiv says Russia hits energy targets despite Trump ceasefire announcement
item.description: Russia hit at least six energy targets during deadly airstrikes across Ukraine, showing it had no interest in an energy ceasefire announced by US President Donald Trump, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said on Monday.
item.dc:creator: Daniel Flynn, Pavel Polityuk
item.content:encoded: Russia hit at least six energy targets during deadly airstrikes across Ukraine, showing it had no interest in an energy ceasefire announced by US President Donald Trump, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said on Monday. Under pressure over high energy prices ahead of US midterm elections next month, Trump blindsided Kyiv and its European allies over the weekend by declaring that Ukraine and Russia had agreed not to hit each other's energy systems. "It is increasingly evident that Russia is unwilling to accept an energy ceasefire proposed by the United States and intends to continue its terrorist air attacks against our people and communities," Zelenskiy said on X. "This is what happens when Russia sees the prospect of higher revenues for its war machine." In earlier comments by video link to a conference in Poland, Zelenskiy identified two of the targets as a gas facility and a petrol station, both hit by Russian drones. Trump announced the purported energy ceasefire days after unveiling a [USN:L4N45Y0AR TEXT:"deal to buy diesel from Russia"], which Zelenskiy has criticised as a reversal of years of Western policy aimed at isolating Russia's economy. Trump, for his part, has called on Ukrainians to unseat Zelenskiy in an election, an unusually severe exchange in a relationship between the two leaders that has been strained since Trump returned to power in 2025. Russian President Vladimir Putin's point man for oil, Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak, [USN:L1N45Y0MF TEXT:"said"] Moscow would be able to return diesel exports to levels above those Trump outlined under the diesel deal. Trump [USN:L1N45Y0QE TEXT:"defended"] the deal as US lawmakers from both major parties complained that it appeared to violate US law. The president's envoys [USN:L1N45Y0OS TEXT:"told Ukrainian officials"] last week that the deal sought to draw Russia back to talks on ending the war, three people familiar with the meeting told Reuters. Trump's weekend announcement on an energy ceasefire was the second time within a few weeks that Trump had issued such a declaration without confirmation from the two warring sides. Ukraine's European allies on Monday voiced scepticism of any such agreement, spoke in support of Kyiv and [USN:L8N45T1J0 TEXT:"approved the largest set of EU sanctions"] since Russia's 2022 invasion. "Russia will only negotiate seriously under pressure, which is why we are sticking to our sanctions against Russia," German Chancellor Friedrich Merz in Berlin. 'WE DO NOT WANT A CEASEFIRE,' KREMLIN SAYS Kyiv has increasingly targeted Russian oil refineries and logistics with long-range strikes, its answer to more than four-and-a-half years of relentless Russian attacks on its cities, including persistent campaigns to knock out Ukraine's power and heat in successive winters. Zelenskiy said Ukraine had carried out no attacks on Russian refineries overnight and was willing to agree an energy ceasefire, but said it was [USN:L8N45Y12U TEXT:""increasingly clear""] Russia would not abide by it. He also said elections, suspended during wartime, could be held if Moscow agreed to a full ceasefire for 60 days. Russia said talks [USN:R4N45F02J TEXT:"were proceeding"] about a possible energy ceasefire, and Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said further information would be revealed in due course. But he rejected Zelenskiy's proposal for a full 60-day truce. "In the Kremlin, both President (Vladimir) Putin and officials at other levels have repeatedly stated that we do not want a ceasefire," said Peskov. "We want long-term peace and are prepared to do everything possible to achieve it." BODY AMONG WRECKAGE In Kyiv, a new Russian strike on a high-rise apartment block killed two people and injured at least nine, while attacks in other regions killed at least six people, officials said. New strikes also targeted Kharkiv, Ukraine's second-biggest city in the northeast. Ukraine's Emergency Services said 11 people had been injured in evening attacks, including one strike which triggered the collapse of an entrance to an apartment building. Overnight attacks killed at least three people in Kharkiv and further strikes in the morning wounded at least 22. Three people were killed near Kramatorsk one of Ukraine's "fortress cities" in eastern Donetsk region that Russian forces have set their sights on in their slow advance westward. In Kharkiv, Nataliia Minka said she had just made it to a shelter when a missile struck nearby. She and her child had seen what they believed to be a missile hitting a power station. "Ten minutes had passed since they promised they wouldn’t target energy facilities," she said. "It’s so hard to describe how a child was lying there, already covered up, and the father was running around her, crying and screaming," she added. Russia began its latest strike campaign on Ukraine's grid two weeks ago, already causing daily, hours-long power cuts in Kyiv, affecting the capital's water and sewage systems and twice bringing its underground trains to an abrupt halt. To maintain pressure on Moscow, European Union foreign ministers on Monday added 1,569 new names to their sanctions list of banned individuals and businesses, billed as the largest single package to date. Trump has increasingly blamed Kyiv's attacks on Russian refineries for surging global costs for fuel, especially diesel, which has hit record U.S prices since he launched his military campaign against Iran. On Saturday, he said Zelenskiy had [USN:L6N45W06G TEXT:""better damn well stop""] attacking Russian refineries.

item.title: Philippine lower house approves bill restricting minors' social media access
item.description: The Philippines on Monday moved a step closer to restricting social media use among minors after its lower house of Congress approved a measure banning access to platforms for children under 13.
item.dc:creator: Nestor Corrales, Mikhail Flores
item.content:encoded: The Philippines on Monday moved a step closer to restricting social media use among minors after its lower house of Congress approved a measure banning access to platforms for children under 13. The Philippines is the latest country, from Greece and Portugal to Australia, [USN:L6N41Z08Z TEXT:"Malaysia "]and [USN:L4N40E0HB TEXT:"Indonesia,"] to try to curb [USN:L8N42Q0MC TEXT:"social media use by minors,"] as concern grows over its effects on child health and safety. The House of Representatives voted overwhelmingly in favour of limiting minors' access to social media platforms, following on from the Senate's recent endorsement of a similar bill. The two chambers will now be required to reconcile their bills then submit a final draft for presidential approval. The progress of the legislation comes after three school shootings since June in the Philippines that reignited [USN:L6N44G0IZ TEXT:"debate"] over children accessing social media and online content. A 16-year-old last month [USN:L4N45A0KH TEXT:"shot dead"] at least two fellow students before turning the gun on himself, while in August, a student [USN:L6N44F03Q TEXT:"live-streamed"] himself shooting and killing a classmate before taking his own life. Gun violence at schools was previously rare in the Philippines. President Ferdinand Marcos Jr said on Sunday he had been studying the bill passed by the Senate and that a blanket ban on social media could cause children to hide their online activities, leaving them vulnerable to grooming and abuse. The Senate's version is stricter than the draft approved by the lower house and bans anyone under 18 from creating social media accounts. TikTok, YouTube owner Alphabet (GOOGL.O) , and Meta Platforms (META.O) , the owner of Facebook and Instagram, did not immediately respond to separate requests for comment on the Philippines house passing the bill. Neighbouring Malaysia in June began barring under-16s from registering accounts on social media platforms, which are required to conduct age verification against government-issued records. Malaysia has given social platforms until January 2027 to implement the measure. Indonesia issued a regulation in March requiring social media firms with platforms it deems high risk to deactivate accounts belonging to children under 16, which have so far included X, Instagram and video game platform Roblox. As of last week, TikTok has deactivated around 9 million accounts belonging to children under 16 in Indonesia, while Meta has blocked 85,000 Instagram accounts and 99,000 Facebook accounts.

FAST

LONDON, Oct 12 : Artificial Intelligence needs urgent global regulation with independent evaluators able to vet new developments, the president of Microsoft said, warning that AI currently faces fewer safety requirements than milk.   In an interview with the BBC published on Monday, Brad Smith said a set of global safety rules needed to be in place, requiring a "victim" to be informed if their system is breached by a rogue AI agent and an "emergency brake" available. He said there should also be a legal requirement for companies to write "incident reports".  "We know how to do this for other products," Smith said. "We should build on that knowledge and think about how to apply it to AI."

"Right now, your washing machine is subject to more safety rules than AI. Every carton of milk that you see in the grocery store is subject to safety rules and inspection." Tech companies such as Anthropic and OpenAI have started disclosing rogue or undesired behaviour by AI agents as part of a global debate about the fast-advancing technology that has included researchers' warnings of an eventual existential threat to humanity. Some companies have called for AI development to slow down, but that has sparked a debate as to whether executives have ulterior motives such as setting rules that preserve the lead of their firms, pre-empting a broader government backlash, or simply slowing breakneck spending. Microsoft's Smith said the one country that was well-placed to lead the way on regulation of AI was Britain, due to the AI Security Institute which was launched under former prime minister, Rishi Sunak.  Smith said officials in Washington viewed London very differently to how they viewed Brussels, which regulates AI based on the level of risk via its AI Act. Britain's institute receives pre-deployment access under voluntary agreements with the major AI models, allowing it to assess their capabilities and risks.  AI Minister Kanishka Narayan has told Reuters that Britain would consider regulating advanced models if the current system proved insufficient.

Source: Reuters
